hooks.text: A six-sided storm wide enough to swallow two Earths spins on Saturn.
Two whole Earths could drop inside a single geometric storm on Saturn.
Nature usually hates straight lines, but Saturn has a massive cloud hexagon.

title: Nature's 20,000-Mile GEOMETRY on Saturn
description: Saturn's north pole features a colossal six-sided jet stream wide enough to swallow two Earths. Here is how nature carves pure geometry into the clouds.

beats.text: A six-sided storm wide enough to swallow two Earths spins on Saturn.
beats.visual: Cassini natural color full view of Saturn's north polar hexagon, 2013

beats.text: NASA's Voyager probes first spotted this geometric jet stream at the planet's north pole.
beats.visual: Voyager 2 polar perspective mosaic of Saturn showing the hexagon, 1981

beats.text: The structure spans 20,000 miles across, wider than two Earths side-by-side.
beats.visual: Diagram comparing the diameter of Earth to the width of Saturn's hexagon, 2014

beats.text: Even more incredible, each single side of the hexagon is longer than Earth’s entire diameter.
beats.visual: Cassini high-resolution view of Saturn's northern cloud bands and hexagon, 2014

card.small: a single side of the hexagon

beats.text: Winds blast at 200 miles per hour around a central hurricane as wide as a continent.
beats.visual: Cassini close-up photograph of the central polar vortex hurricane eye, 2012

beats.text: Over decades, the vortex shifted from deep blue to golden yellow as sunlight reacted with methane.
beats.visual: Cassini side-by-side color comparison showing Saturn's hexagon shifting colors, 2016

beats.text: This isn't magic—scientists recreated the exact shape in simple water tanks using basic physics.
beats.visual: Laboratory experiment photograph of a fluid tank generating a rotating polygon wave, 2010

beats.text: It proves nature's laws can carve perfect straight lines across an entire planet.
beats.visual: Cassini wide-angle mosaic of Saturn and its rings viewed from above the northern hemisphere, 2013
